title: 3D Atlas: Glucose and peptide connections
question: How can molecular connections help explain different biological materials?
explanation: Inspect schematic glucose and peptide models. Glucose has six carbons overall; its common six-membered ring includes one oxygen. Water interactions and carbon bonding are explained in the chapter.
limits: Schematic teaching geometry; this scene does not show an ice lattice or simulate freezing.

title: 3D Atlas: Glucose-derived building units
question: Why can polymers built from glucose-derived units have different properties?
explanation: Compare the glucose building unit with the chapter’s starch, glycogen and cellulose plate. Link orientation and branching matter; the monomer model alone cannot establish polymer properties.
limits: Schematic monomer and peptide models, not an interactive alpha/beta polymer conversion.

title: 3D Atlas: Backbone restrictions and protein folding
question: Why can a protein sketch preserve the amino-acid sequence yet propose an impossible shape?
explanation: Inspect a chosen two-basin backbone-angle surface and a schematic chain. Local crowding restricts arrangements; a local angle map does not predict every complete protein fold.
limits: Invented illustrative surface, not measured atomic energies or the original Ramachandran map. Real maps vary with amino-acid type.

title: 3D Atlas: Enzyme binding and a chosen rate model
question: Why does substrate binding alone not establish that a protein catalyses a reaction?
explanation: Inspect an invented enzyme cleft and compare chosen Michaelis–Menten rate responses to substrate and inhibitor. The chapter explains the separate activation-barrier account.
limits: Abstract shapes and chosen steady-state kinetics; no measured lactase rates, atomic docking or directly simulated transition state.

title: 3D Atlas: An illustrative temperature response
question: Why can warming first increase a reaction rate and later reduce it?
explanation: Change the chosen temperature parameter and compare relative model activity. The picture changes shape at a declared model threshold; this is not a universal protein failure temperature.
limits: No exposure-time history or pH slider here. Relative activity is not measured native-fold fraction; the model cannot establish irreversible damage or diagnose fever.

title: 3D Atlas: Five food-test examples
question: What comparisons make a food-test result interpretable?
explanation: Inspect five schematic positive examples: iodine, Benedict’s, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP. Compare their targets with the chapter’s table and keep known positives, blanks and untreated samples in a real investigation.
limits: Schematic rack, not actual chemical measurements or a control experiment. All reagent procedures belong in a supervised school laboratory.

title: 3D Atlas: Photosynthetic material account
question: How can atmospheric carbon become plant material?
explanation: Compare the formal net-equation mass account with the chapter’s carbon journey from CO₂ to sugars and cell walls.
limits: Formal net balance, not a dry-mass measurement of van Helmont’s tree or an atom-route simulation; water also supplies matter.

title: 3D Atlas: Aquatic plant gas observation
question: Why does net oxygen release not measure gross photosynthesis?
explanation: Inspect a modern schematic plant jar and chosen net-output markers. The chapter’s tracer evidence identifies water as the released oxygen source.
limits: Not a reconstruction of Ingenhousz’s apparatus or calibrated bubbles; markers vanish at nonpositive chosen net output.

title: 3D Atlas: Chloroplast compartments
question: How do light-supported reactions supply carbon-building reactions?
explanation: Inspect thylakoid stacks and surrounding stroma. Light-supported machinery supplies ATP and NADPH; carbon fixation supplies small organic products.
limits: The glucose model represents a later overall summary product, not the immediate product of the carbon-fixation cycle; no electron-transfer kinetics are simulated.

title: 3D Atlas: Invented limiting-factor surface
question: Why can increasing one input sometimes leave the rate unchanged?
explanation: Vary chosen light and CO₂ capacities and temperature to inspect a simple minimum-capacity model. Net output subtracts a chosen respiratory baseline 10.
limits: Invented capacities and 25 °C peak, not a fitted Farquhar model, actual concentrations or universal plant optimum.

title: 3D Atlas: Representative leaf structure
question: How do leaf structures support light capture, gas exchange and water balance?
explanation: Inspect palisade columns, a guard-cell pair and adjacent vascular tubes. Connect the schematic to the chapter’s full leaf cross-section.
limits: Selected representative structures, not a complete anatomical specimen or measured light-attenuation model.

title: 3D Atlas: Leaf water loss and xylem
question: How does leaf evaporation contribute to water flow through connected xylem?
explanation: Inspect the guard-cell and vascular schematic, then trace the chapter’s evaporation, tension and replacement-water chain.
limits: Chosen aperture and transport-activity values are illustrative, not measured speeds or a universal response to light.

title: 3D Atlas: Phloem source–sink flow
question: Why can phloem carry sugars upwards or downwards in different pathways?
explanation: Compare the vascular tubes with the chapter’s loading, osmotic entry, pressure-driven flow and unloading account.
limits: Tube schematic and invented relative activity; not a Poiseuille solver. Opposite bulk streams do not share one tube at the same moment; loading routes vary.

title: 3D Atlas: Glycolytic Carbon Splitting & Controlled Oxidation Staircase
question: Why must glycolysis invest 2 ATP at the top of the staircase before harvesting 4 ATP and 2 NADH from splitting a 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvates?
explanation: Following the 6-carbon chain in 3D shows phosphorylation priming and destabilising the hexose ring so aldolase can cleave it cleanly into two triose phosphates that yield a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
limits: Ten enzymatic steps condensed into the key 6C → 2 × 3C cleavage geometry.

title: 3D Atlas: Mitochondrial Cristae & Krebs Tricarboxylic Wheel
question: How do the folded inner cristae and central matrix of the mitochondrion divide the work of the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation?
explanation: Using Section cutaway mode on the 3D mitochondrion exposes the central matrix—where the 8-step Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA to CO₂ while loading NADH and FADH₂—surrounded by deeply folded cristae packed with electron-transport complexes.
limits: Idealised lamellar cristae folds for clear cross-sectional viewing.

title: 3D Atlas: Rotary F₀F₁-ATP Synthase Molecular Turbine
question: How does a transmembrane proton gradient physically turn a protein rotor to forge ~26–28 ATP per glucose molecule?
explanation: Exploding the 3D F₀F₁-ATP synthase reveals protons flowing down Δp (~180 mV) through the membrane c-ring rotor, spinning the asymmetric γ-shaft in 120° steps inside the catalytic α₃β₃ hexamer to press ADP + P_i into ATP.

title: 3D Atlas: Where Exhaled Carbon Mass Exits in the Krebs Cycle
question: When you lose body mass during exercise, how do the carbon and oxygen atoms actually leave your body?
explanation: Inspecting the 3D pyruvate dehydrogenase and Krebs cycle decarboxylation steps in the mitochondrial matrix shows all 6 carbons of glucose exiting as exhaled CO₂ gas while O₂ accepts electrons at Complex IV to form metabolic H₂O.
limits: Stoichiometric C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O balance.

title: 3D Atlas: Lactic & Alcoholic Fermentation NAD⁺ Rescue Fork
question: Why does a cell deprived of oxygen get stuck at just 2 ATP per glucose and convert pyruvate into lactate or ethanol?
explanation: Lowering O₂ partial pressure in the 3D fermentation fork shows Complex IV stalling; to keep cytosolic NAD⁺ from running out—which would halt glycolysis—pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH to form lactate or ethanol + CO₂.
limits: Pasteur-effect switch modelled as a smooth Hill function of pO₂.

title: 3D Atlas: Waterlogged Root Hypoxia & ATP Starvation
question: Why do over-watered pot plants wilt and yellow even though their roots are submerged in water?
explanation: Dialing down O₂ in the 3D respiration and ATP synthase stations shows root mitochondria stalling from 30 ATP to 2 ATP per glucose in anoxic soil, starving the root-hair proton pumps needed for mineral and water uptake.
limits: Steady-state normoxic vs hypoxic ATP yield comparison.
